topic: Robert Hampson, Dong Song, Sam Deadwyler & Theodore Berger (2018): Hippocampal CA3-to-CA1 MIMO Memory Prosthesis
visual_mode_reason: The entire study takes place via depth microelectrodes implanted inside human hippocampal subfields CA3 and CA1, translating real-time spike trains through a nonlinear MIMO model and writing electrical patterns back into CA1.

primary_case.title: Closed-loop human hippocampal CA3-to-CA1 MIMO neural prosthesis trial (37% short-term & 35% delayed recall boost)
primary_case.place: Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center (Winston-Salem, NC) & University of Southern California (Los Angeles)

core_facts.fact: In 2018 in the Journal of Neural Engineering, Robert Hampson, Dong Song, Sam Deadwyler, Theodore Berger, and colleagues tested a closed-loop hippocampal memory prosthesis in 17 surgical epilepsy patients (8 subset in full closed-loop stimulation).
Patients already had bilateral depth electrodes with microscopic microwires implanted into hippocampal subfields CA3 (input layer) and CA1 (output layer) for clinical seizure mapping.
Conventional constant-frequency deep brain stimulation fails or even impairs episodic memory because real hippocampal encoding relies on precise spatiotemporal spike patterns, not flat pulses.

During Phase 1, patients played a delayed match-to-sample (DMS) visual memory game on a touchscreen while researchers recorded single-neuron spike trains simultaneously in CA3 and CA1 on successful recall trials.

Dong Song's multi-input, multi-output (MIMO) nonlinear Volterra model learned each individual patient's mathematical transfer function predicting healthy CA1 output spikes from incoming CA3 input spikes.

During Phase 2 stimulation trials, as a patient viewed a sample image, the prosthesis read live CA3 spikes and delivered biphasic microampere pulses patterned to match predicted CA1 firing directly into CA1.
Playing the personalized MIMO code into CA1 boosted short-term delayed-match-to-sample memory performance by an average of 37 percent over non-stimulated baseline trials.
On a separate delayed recognition test conducted up to 75 minutes later (long-term retention), items encoded with MIMO stimulation showed a 35 percent memory improvement.

Control trials delivering randomized/scrambled pulse patterns at identical total current produced zero memory gain, proving the specific spatiotemporal code — not generic electrical arousal — drove the 37% boost.
In 2024, Roeder and colleagues extended the human prosthesis using stimulus-feature codes, improving recall in over half of participants and especially those with baseline impaired memory.

In Hampson, Song, Deadwyler, and Berger (2018), 17 epilepsy patients implanted with CA3-to-CA1 microwires showed +37% short-term and +35% 75-minute delayed recognition gains under MIMO stimulation, compared with 0% gain under random/scrambled control pulses.

wow_facts.fact: Writing a patient's own mathematical CA3-to-CA1 spike code back into their hippocampus boosted short-term visual memory by 37 percent and 75-minute delayed recall by 35 percent.
wow_facts.why_surprising: It was the first time scientists wrote a personalized neural memory code back into the human brain to strengthen real recall.

wow_facts.fact: Delivering the exact same electrical energy in a scrambled random rhythm gave zero benefit.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Memory is a temporal melody, not a voltage battery — only the right rhythm unlocks CA1.

wow_facts.fact: The computer never needed to know whether the patient was looking at a house, a flower, or a landscape — it translated pure CA3 spike timing into CA1 spike timing.
wow_facts.why_surprising: The MIMO chip acted like a biological synaptic bridge speaking native hippocampal dialect.

wow_facts.fact: A 2024 follow-up trial showed the biggest memory rescue occurred in patients who started with clinically impaired baseline memory.
wow_facts.why_surprising: That points directly toward future prosthetics for traumatic brain injury and early dementia.

misconceptions.myth: The memory chip uploads fake movie memories like The Matrix or Total Recall.
misconceptions.truth: The prosthesis cannot implant foreign memories; it only reinforces the CA3-to-CA1 synaptic handoff of what the patient is genuinely looking at right now.

misconceptions.myth: More electricity always equals better memory.
misconceptions.truth: Flat continuous high-frequency stimulation often disrupts hippocampal encoding; microampere patterned timing is what works.

misconceptions.myth: One universal memory code can be copied straight from one person's brain into another's without tuning.
misconceptions.truth: In the 2018 trial, every MIMO model was fit individually to each patient's own CA3-CA1 microwire geometry.

misconceptions.myth: The chip stores memories permanently on silicon.
misconceptions.truth: The chip acts as a real-time encoding bridge so the patient's own neocortex and hippocampus consolidate the memory naturally, lasting 75+ minutes after stimulation ends.

everyday_hooks: Walking out of a parking garage and realizing the floor number vanished because your tired brain dropped the handoff during encoding.
Studying a flashcard when distracted versus locking it in crisply on the first look.
Hearing a hearing aid clarify speech syllables rather than just cranking up loud static.
Meeting someone at an event and forgetting their name ten seconds later because CA3-to-CA1 encoding faltered.
